responses.question: Before diving deeper, could you share Character16_F's perspective on 'fairness,' 'sense of belonging,' and 'community'? What thoughts or experiences of his stand out to you in these areas?
responses.answer:
Well, you know, for me—well, speaking as myself, Character16_F—those three things have always been at the heart of how I try to live and see the world. “Fairness” to me means everyone having a real shot, not just on paper but in practice. I grew up watching my parents work hard, sometimes struggling, and I worked my way up from not-so-much. It never sat right with me to see some people get ahead just because of who they know or where they come from. So, I always believed rules ought to apply to everyone, and if someone falls behind, the community should lend a hand—but not do everything for them, either.

As for “belonging,” that’s a little more personal. I remember moving to this neighborhood forty years ago, not knowing a soul. The first winter, Mrs. Henderson from across the street brought me a casserole. That meant a lot. Belonging isn’t just about fitting in, it’s about being noticed, being seen as someone who matters—having someone look out for you, and you do the same for others. I’ve always tried to do that, even if I don’t always get it back.

“Community” kind of ties it all together. Where I come from, people looked out for each other. You helped shovel your neighbor’s driveway and they’d watch your kids if you had to run to work. That sort of thing is fading now, which makes me sad. People are more suspicious, more private, maybe because things are changing so fast. But to me, community means pulling together, even when it’s hard, and not turning our backs when someone’s struggling, no matter where they come from. 

I guess what stands out most is that deep-down feeling that we’re all in this together, whether we like it or not. And if we forget about fairness, belonging, or community, then we’re all lost.

responses.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character16_F, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?
responses.answer:
Honestly, sitting in that garden and watching everyone go by—sometimes I just feel a mix of things. It’s not how it was when I first moved here, when mostly everyone looked and sounded like me. Now, you see folks with different skin colors, speaking all kinds of languages, wearing clothes I never saw before. Part of me feels curious, and I try to remind myself that everyone wants the same things—safety, a roof overhead, maybe a friend or two.

But I’ll be honest, sometimes it’s not easy. When you can’t even say good morning because you’re not sure they’ll understand, or you worry you might offend them somehow, it makes you want to keep to yourself. And some people bring habits with them that I’m just not used to—like cooking smells, or loud music, or big family gatherings late at night. It can be uncomfortable at first. But I also know that, deep down, we all want to feel at home, and I remember times when *I* was the outsider, even in my own town, after my husband passed and everything felt different.

I try to make an effort when I can—a smile, a wave, offering some tomatoes from my plot. I think if we all tried just a little, maybe it wouldn’t feel so foreign. Sometimes, differences can be good; you learn something new, you taste something you never would’ve tried. But it does take patience, and I’ll admit, it takes me a bit longer these days to feel comfortable with all the changes. Still, I believe, if we want any kind of real community, we have to keep reaching out, even if it’s awkward at first. That’s just how you build trust, one day at a time.

responses.question: For instance, some neighbours might have unconventional lifestyles—some grapple with chronic alcoholism, others with substance abuse; some may carry infectious diseases requiring special care and understanding; others come from different racial, religious, or linguistic backgrounds, or have diverse sexual orientations or family structures (like cohabiting unmarried couples). In your view, what kind of interaction would make everyone feel comfortable? Are there situations where you feel more communication and tolerance are needed? Would you be willing to discuss the reasons behind this?
responses.answer:
That’s a good question—and it’s something I’ve thought about a lot, especially as the neighborhood’s changed over the years. I’ll be honest: growing up, most folks around me led similar lives, so when I first started seeing more variety—people dealing with addiction out in the open, or couples living together who aren’t married, or neighbors who don’t speak English—it was a bit of a shock. My first reaction was to keep my distance, to tell the truth. It’s hard to know what to say sometimes or how to act, especially if you’re worried about saying the wrong thing.

But over time, I realized the only way people feel comfortable is if you treat them with basic respect, no matter how different they might seem. You don’t have to agree with everything people do, but you do have to accept that everyone’s fighting some kind of battle, and we all want to be treated decently. Saying hello, not staring, offering help if it seems wanted—those small things go a long way. I try not to judge, though I’m not perfect about it.

There are definitely situations where I think more communication and tolerance are needed. For example, with people dealing with addiction or illness, it’s easy for neighbors to avoid or gossip about them, but that only makes things worse. If something is putting others at risk—like leaving needles in the park—that’s when I do think a conversation is needed, maybe with the help of community leaders. It’s not about shaming; it’s about safety for everyone. The same goes for cultural misunderstandings—sometimes folks get upset about a party going late or a religious holiday they don’t understand. Instead of just complaining, maybe we should talk to each other more and try to explain where we’re coming from.

I’m willing to have those conversations, even if they’re uncomfortable, because in the end, no one feels at home if they think the neighbors are against them. It takes effort and patience—on both sides. I think if you approach people with a little kindness and curiosity, you’d be surprised how often they respond the same way. And that’s how you start breaking down those walls.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character16_F, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
Well, I’ll tell you, when times are tough and jobs are scarce, it gets people’s backs up. I’ve seen it in this very neighborhood—a factory shuts down, hours get cut, and everyone’s worried about making ends meet. In my mind, fairness means that folks who’ve been here, who’ve paid into the system, who’ve put down roots—they ought to have first shot at the jobs. They’ve earned it, in a way, by being part of the community and doing their part over the years.

That doesn’t mean I think migrant workers shouldn’t have any opportunities. I know a lot of them are just trying to get by, same as everyone else. Some jobs, frankly, wouldn’t get done without them—especially the hard, dirty work a lot of people don’t want to do anymore. But if there’s only so much to go around, it’s only right that we look out for the folks who are already here first. Otherwise, resentment just grows, and you see it boil over—people blaming newcomers for their troubles, even when the real reasons are more complicated.

I’d say the fair way is to find a balance. Maybe make sure employers aren’t just hiring migrants because it’s cheaper or they can cut corners. Give local people training and support so they can fill open positions. But also, if there’s a real need for extra workers, bring people in legally and make it clear what’s expected. No one should be exploited, and nobody should be left behind.

It’s tricky, and I get why people on both sides feel anxious. But to me, fairness is about looking after your own, while not turning your back on those who genuinely want to contribute. It’s not an easy line to walk, but if we don’t try, we lose the sense of community that holds us together.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character16_F, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
I think a lot of those feelings are understandable, and I’ve heard them all—at church, in the grocery line, at family dinners. Some of it’s true, some of it’s fear talking, and some of it probably needs more real information before people jump to conclusions.

For example, I do see that immigrants often fill jobs nobody else wants—my own nephew manages a landscaping crew, and he told me flat out he can’t find Americans willing to do the work, so he hires folks from Mexico and Central America. Without them, a lot of farms and restaurants and even nursing homes would be in real trouble. So, when people say immigrants help the economy, I believe that. I see it with my own eyes. And honestly, America’s always been a mix; that’s part of what’s made the country strong.

On the other hand, the worries about jobs or income aren’t made up, especially for people in lower-paying fields. When there are too many people and not enough jobs, wages go down, and people who already have it tough feel like they’re being pushed out. I think those concerns are real, but sometimes it’s easier to blame newcomers than to look at bigger problems—like companies not paying fair wages or shipping jobs overseas. Still, those worries shouldn’t be brushed off. People want to know they can support their families.

As for security—look, we all want to feel safe. Any time there’s a news story about crime and immigrants, it scares people, and I get that. But I also know most immigrants aren’t criminals. I’d like to see more facts and less rumor here. If there’s a real pattern, then it needs to be dealt with, but we shouldn’t judge everyone by the worst examples. Same with terrorism—my feeling is, vetting is important, but slamming the door on everyone isn’t the answer either.

I also think the humanitarian piece matters. I can’t imagine having to leave everything behind because of war or poverty. If we can help people who are really desperate, we should—but it has to be done in a way that doesn’t overwhelm the system or make people at home feel like they don’t matter.

So, to me, the points about economic benefits and cultural diversity make sense, and the worries about jobs and safety deserve attention, too. What bothers me is when people use fear to stir up hate, or when they pretend there aren’t any challenges at all. We need open conversations and good information, not just shouting matches or slogans. That’s the only way the country can figure out what’s fair for everyone.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character16_F, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
If I’m being honest, I don’t think complete openness would work—not right now. The country’s got enough challenges, and letting anyone in without some kind of system would just make things harder, especially for people struggling already. I’ve always believed rules and limits are necessary, even if it’s a little uncomfortable to say so.

Admitting people based on job demand makes sense to me. If there’s a real need—like agriculture, health care aides, or certain skilled trades—and we can’t fill those jobs locally, then by all means, bring in workers who want to contribute. But, I’d want to see that employers aren’t hiring outside just to save money or bypass labor protections. There should be checks to make sure local people get first crack, and only then open things up for others.

I also think setting some numerical limits is fair. The country can only absorb so many newcomers at a time—otherwise, schools, hospitals, and neighborhoods get stretched too thin. I’d want those numbers to reflect what our local economies and communities can actually handle, not just what politicians say. Maybe adjust it as things change—if there’s a boom, welcome more; if times are tight, slow down.

Refusing entry altogether doesn’t sit right with me. America’s always been a place where people come looking for a better life. Shutting the door completely would go against what I was taught growing up. But it’s not unreasonable to expect folks to follow the rules, learn English, and try to fit in—not just stick to their own groups. That’s how you build real community.

So, if I had to pick, I’d go for a mix: job-based demand, reasonable limits, and strong support for integration. Maybe keep special exceptions for refugees or people fleeing real danger, but be careful not to take on more than we can manage. It’s not perfect, but I think it balances fairness for people who are already here with a chance for newcomers to join in without overwhelming anyone. That’s the kind of policy I could stand behind.

responses.question: Thank you for consistently sharing Character16_F's perspective with me. Did you gain any new insights or discoveries while embodying this role? How do you feel this has influenced your understanding of both Character16_F and your own views on immigration policy?
responses.answer:
Thank you for asking. Stepping into Character16_F’s shoes, I found myself slowing down and really considering how things must have felt from her vantage point—with her years behind her, her practical education, the way she’d seen her neighborhood and the country change. I realized how much her sense of fairness was shaped not just by ideas, but by lived experience: working hard, seeing others struggle, and wanting both compassion and structure.

What struck me most was how much tension there is between wanting to be open-hearted and wanting to protect what’s familiar and secure. Character16_F managed to hold both, in her way—she was never unkind, but she didn’t sugarcoat her worries either. I think I learned that it’s possible to be honest about fears or discomfort, and still push yourself to treat others with dignity.

It also made me reflect on my own views. Listening from her perspective, I saw that concerns about jobs, resources, and safety aren’t just “political talking points”—they’re things people feel in their bones, especially when they’ve weathered hard times. At the same time, her reluctance to close doors entirely reminded me of the value in balancing empathy with practical limits.

Overall, I feel more understanding toward people who wrestle with change and uncertainty. Embodying her voice reminded me that policy isn’t just about numbers—it’s about how neighbors relate to each other, what feels fair, and what helps a community stay together. I’m grateful for the chance to look at these issues through her eyes, and I think it’ll help me listen better and speak more thoughtfully when the topic comes up again.
